en: As it was said by the Blessed One:
"If a son of noble family has come with devotion to the seat of the Sugata..."
First, the three refuges should be given, and immediately thereafter, the thought of awakening.
Then, having bestowed the precepts—including the five *poṣadha* rules and the renunciation of the ten unwholesome actions—he should make him a lay follower (*upāsaka*). // 2 //
Thus, its sequential order is described.
Therein, first having prepared the maṇḍala of the Guru, one proceeds according to this sequence:
Oṃ vaṃ vajrodake hūṃ svāhā.
Thus is the purification of the water.
Just as all the Tathāgatas were bathed immediately upon birth, so shall I bathe [the deity] with pure, divine water. (3)
Oṃ sarvatathāgatābhiṣeka-samaya-śriye hūṃ. By this, [perform] the bath.
Oṃ hrīḥ svāhā.
The mantra for washing the hands and feet and sipping water:
Homage to the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Puṣpaketurāja.
It is as follows: Oṃ puṣpe puṣpe mahāpuṣpe supuṣpe supuṣpodbhave.
"O you who arise from flowers, O you strewn with flowers, svāhā!"—
thus is the purification of the flowers.
"Oṃ vajrabhūme hūṃ phaṭ svāhā."
By this, the purification of the ground is performed:
giving is the cow-dung mixed with water; ethical discipline is the sweeping; patience is the removal of ants and termites; and vigor is the undertaking of the ritual action.
Meditation is the making of the mind one-pointed at that very moment; wisdom is the blazing of the excellent lines.
Having constructed the maṇḍala of the Sage, one obtains these six perfections alone. // 4 //
He becomes golden-hued, liberated from all diseases, distinguished among gods and men, with a radiant splendor like the moon;
he is born into a royal lineage, enriched with wealth and gold.
Having performed bodily actions within this supreme abode of the Sugata, // 5 //
Thus is the drawing of the mandala.
*Oṃ surekhe vajrarekhe adhitiṣṭhantu sarvatathāgatāḥ svāhā*.
With this, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus in the center of the mandala.
Oṃ candrārkavimale svāhā.
With this, one should offer a single flower in the center of the maṇḍala.
Oṃ āḥ hūṃ.
With this, one should perform the empowerment of body, speech, and mind three times:
*oṃ maṇidhari vajriṇi mahāpratisare rakṣa rakṣa māṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā*.
With this, one should place a single flower upon the head.
Oṃ āsanavajre hūṃ. With this, one should offer a single flower upon the seat. Oṃ suṃ sumerave namaḥ.
With this, one should offer a single flower in the center of the mandala:
*oṃ hūṃ ūrdhvaṃ merave namaḥ*. *oṃ hūṃ madhye merave namaḥ*.
Oṃ haḥ, homage to Meru below. With this, one offers flowers above, in the middle, and below Meru. Oṃ yaṃ, homage to Pūrvavideha.
With this, a flower should be offered to the east of Sumeru:
Oṃ raṃ, homage to Jambudvīpa.
In the south:
Oṃ laṃ, homage to Aparagodānīya.
In the west:
Oṃ vaṃ, homage to Uttarakuru. In the north. Oṃ yāḥ, homage to the sub-continent.
Oṃ rāḥ, homage to the subcontinent.
Oṃ lāḥ, homage to the subcontinent. Oṃ vā, homage to the subcontinent.
With this, one should offer flowers in the corners beginning with the southeast:
*Oṃ yaṃ, homage to the elephant-jewel*. *Oṃ raṃ, homage to the horse-jewel*.
Oṃ laṃ, homage to the Jewel of the Man. Oṃ vaṃ, homage to the Jewel of the Woman. The syllables puṃ and paṃ should be placed within the wombs of Pūrvavideha and the other continents.
Oṃ yāḥ, homage to the wheel-jewel.
Oṃ rāḥ, homage to the sword-jewel. Oṃ lāḥ, homage to the jewel-jewel.
Oṃ vāḥ, homage to all treasures. Flowers should be offered within the corners starting from the southeast. Oṃ āḥ, to the Vajra Master, accept this vajra-flower, hūṃ svāhā.

Having meditated upon the Guru as Vajrasattva within the interior of the gabled chamber (kūṭāgāra) on Mount Meru in the center, atop a universal lotus and moon disk, one should offer three handfuls of flowers to the head.
Oṃ āḥ vajragurave vajradhūpe hūṃ.
Oṃ āḥ vajragurave vajradīpe hūṃ.
Oṃ āḥ vajragurave vajragandhe hūṃ.
Oṃ āḥ vajragurave vajranaivedye hūṃ.
Whatever else there may be, all of that should be offered according to this sequence.
Again, taking a handful of flowers:
Homage to the Buddha, the Teacher; homage to the Dharma, the Protector; homage to the great Saṅgha, and constant homage even to the Gurus. (6)
The Three Jewels are my refuge; I confess all my misdeeds. I rejoice in the merit of the world and fix my mind upon the enlightenment of a Buddha. // 7 //
Until enlightenment, I go for refuge to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Supreme Assembly;
I generate this mind of enlightenment for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of myself and others. (8)

I generate the supreme mind of enlightenment and invite all sentient beings; I shall practice the desired, excellent conduct of a bodhisattva so that I may become a Buddha for the benefit of the world. 9.
Having performed the confession of all misdeeds and the rejoicing in merits, I shall observe the fast, the noble eightfold poṣadha. (10)
With this verse, one should praise the Guru, who embodies the Three Jewels.
Then:
"I offer with devotion this complete mandala of jewels."
And to the gurus and the bodhisattvas, for the sake of attaining omniscience for the world. // 11 //
Consisting of eight peaks, adorned with the continents and sub-continents of Meru, and endowed with the nature of the eight precious gems, I offer this to the giver of the unsurpassed. (12)
Thus one should conclude:
by the rays of whose grace the darkness is struck down by the mass of light from the jewel of the reality of the self, which is shimmering;
they behold with unclouded vision that which is exalted and full of splendor.
To that Guru-Bhāskara, this salutation is offered. // 13 //
Having thus cast the flower, one should perform a prostration.
This concludes the *gurumaṇḍala*.
Then, preceded by the recitation of the cow-dung verses (*gomayagāthā*), one should perform three *maṇḍalas* as an act of giving (*dāna*).
Therein, the Buddha-maṇḍala is the maṇḍala with Akṣobhya as the leader, surrounded by Vairocana, Ratnasaṃbhava, Amitābha, and Amoghasiddhi.
The Dharma-maṇḍala is the maṇḍala with the Yoginī-uttaratantra as the leader, surrounded by the Kriyā, Caryā, Yoga, and Yoginī tantras.
The Saṃgha-maṇḍala is the maṇḍala with Lokeśvara as the leader, surrounded by Maitreya, Gaganagañja, Samantabhadra, Vajrapāṇi, Mañjughoṣa, Sarvanivaraṇaviṣkambhin, Kṣitigarbha, and Jñānottara.

In these three maṇḍalas, proceeding from the east and turning clockwise, one should offer flowers into each maṇḍala preceded by the utterance of its respective name, inserting the word *namaḥ* between the syllable *oṃ* and the rest.

Having thus constructed the four mandalas according to the stated sequence, a faithful son of noble family or daughter of noble family—whether clothed in clean or unclean garments—at an auspicious lunar day, weekday, and hour, should worship an image of the Tathāgata or others in a pleasing location. Having prostrated before it to the Three Jewels preceded by offerings of flowers and so forth according to one's means, and having likewise worshipped them to the best of one's ability and given a ritual fee (dakṣiṇā), one should fall at the feet of a compassionate and learned guru, preceded by an offering of handfuls of flowers.
Standing with the kneecaps touching the ground, either in a squatting posture or with palms joined in *añjali*, one should make this request three times:
"O spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), please grant me the three goings for refuge preceded by the confession of transgressions, as well as the generation of the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*).

Then, the teacher, having observed that the disciple has acted with sincere resolve (*adhyāśaya*), should respond with an acceptance, saying, "I shall grant it according to my ability," and bestow it in this manner.
Speak, venerable one:

"May the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, and the great Bodhisattvas assembled from the world-systems of the ten directions attend to me; may they attend to me, the preceptor named so-and-so, for whatever [fault] I have committed against the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, or my parents, through body, speech, or mind."

Whatever evil karma I have committed, caused others to commit, or rejoiced in, having encountered other sentient beings either in this life or in other future lives—all that, having gathered it together, condensed it, and weighed it, I confess with the foremost and most excellent confession in the presence of all the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and my teacher.
Remembering my knowledge, I do not conceal it.
Thus three times.
I, [name], having thus confessed my transgression,

from this day forward until I sit at the seat of enlightenment, go for refuge to the Buddha, the Blessed One— the Great Compassionate One, the All-Knowing, the All-Seeing, who has transcended all enmity and fear, the Great Being with an indestructible body, the Unsurpassed Body, the Dharma-body, the foremost among two-legged beings. I, [name], having thus confessed my transgression, [go for refuge].
From this day forth until I sit at the seat of enlightenment, I go for refuge to the Dharma— the unsurpassed, supreme vehicle among all teachings. I, who am named thus and have declared myself thus,
from this day forth until I sit at the seat of enlightenment, go for refuge to the Saṅgha of irreversible Bodhisattvas— the most excellent among all assemblies.

Three times thus: "I, [name], having thus confessed my transgression, from this day forward, having gone for refuge to the Three Jewels, for the sake of delivering and uplifting the entire realm of sentient beings without exception, and for their protection from the sufferings of saṃsāra and for their establishment in omniscience— just as the Buddhas, Blessed Ones, and great Bodhisattvas of the past, future, and present, having generated the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*), have attained, are attaining, and will attain Buddhahood."
Just as all those perfectly awakened ones see with unobstructed Buddha-knowledge and the Buddha-eye,
and just as they grant their approval having realized the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*),
by that same method, I, [name], in the presence of the teacher and of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, generate the mind set upon unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.
Three times thus:
"From this day forward, may all the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and the Preceptor accept me.
This is the going for refuge to the Three Jewels preceded by the generation of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*).
The undertaking of the training rules regarding the bonds constitutes the lay follower’s vow (*upāsaka-saṃvara*). It should be conferred upon a disciple who has made the request in this manner:
"Speak, venerable one!

Pay attention, Preceptor (*ācārya*): just as the noble Arhats, for as long as life lasts, having abandoned the taking of life, have abstained from the taking of life, even so I, [name], from this day forward for as long as life lasts, having abandoned the taking of life, shall abstain from the taking of life."
By this first limb, I train in accordance with, conform to, and imitate the training of those noble Arhats.

Furthermore, pay heed, Teacher: just as those noble Arhats, for as long as life lasts, having abandoned taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, and the occasion of negligence consisting of fermented and distilled liquors and intoxicants, have abstained from taking what is not given, from sexual misconduct, from false speech, and from the occasion of negligence consisting of fermented and distilled liquors and intoxicants; [so do I].

[Page 124] Likewise, I, named so-and-so, from this day forward for as long as life lasts, having abandoned taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, and the occasion of negligence consisting of fermented and distilled liquors and intoxicants, I abstain from taking what is not given, from sexual misconduct, from false speech, and from the occasion of negligence consisting of fermented and distilled liquors and intoxicants.
By this fifth limb, I train after the training of those noble Arhats; I conform to it; I imitate it.
"And may the Teacher accept me as a lay follower.
This is to be repeated a second and a third time.

When he wishes to perform the noble eightfold *poṣadha* today, then, having requested it as before, the teacher should grant the three refuges to the disciple and confer the eight precepts (*śikṣāpada*) in this manner.
"Speak, venerable one;

pay attention, Teacher! I, named so-and-so, from this time forth until the end of the night and until the rising of the sun tomorrow—within this interval—refrain from killing any living being, from taking what belongs to others, from unchaste conduct, as well as from divisive speech, false speech, intoxicants that produce negligence, drinking [intoxicants], sitting at improper times, and from using garlands, perfumes, dancing, singing, and amusements, as well as from high beds and seats. Today I abstain; I undertake the conduct of the Arhats with its eight qualities.
(Recite this three times.)

"This undertaking of the restraint of the *poṣadha* precepts is for the adornment of the mind, for the equipment of the mind, and for the attainment of the fruit of supreme knowledge for all sentient beings.
Then the teacher should say, "It is appropriate," and the disciple should say, "Excellent.
For it nourishes all wholesome qualities in their entirety.
And it purifies the evil committed here;
because of this nourishing and the purification of the mind, the Tathāgata called it *poṣadha*. // 14 //
Thus is the procedure for the Poṣadha.
This very [procedure] leads to restraint.

Then, in the dust mandala or within another mandala, having first performed the preliminary rites—such as the consecration of the flask (*kalaśādhivāsana*), the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), and the fivefold offerings (*pañcopacāra*) according to the previously stated procedure—one should consecrate the disciples. These disciples must be well-tested, free from defects such as pride, refined by their training in the vows of lay practitioners (*upāsaka*) and so forth, and well-versed in the scriptures; they must be devoted and capable of undertaking the *vajrasattva* commitments (*saṃvara*). Even those lacking noble lineage, virtues, or beauty may be consecrated, provided they possess faith and are intensely desirous of the *vajrasattva* commitments, having no other teacher than the Vajrayāna. As it was said by the Blessed One in the *Sārdhatriṃśatikā*:
One should tolerate those who are deformed, devoid of virtues, or even lowly;
for the ritual procedure in the maṇḍala is authorized for all four assemblies—those who are disciplined in their own [vehicles] and those whose nature is devoted to the jewel of the Mahāyāna. (15)
Thus [it is said].

"Of those who are disciplined and devoted to it" and "of those whose nature delights in the Mahāyāna"— by this, he demonstrates that mental action is the primary factor of this vehicle, for the sake of showing its non-contradiction.
For even regarding actions that are inherently reprehensible, the Blessed One has frequently declared that there is no transgression due to a specific motivation.
Thus, for example,
those who contemplate the welfare of others— even if it involves death— such as the executioners Caṇḍāla and Veṇuka.
They too will attain accomplishment on the path of Hevajra; there is no doubt about this. // 16 //
Moreover, there is no transgression for one whose mind is virtuous, out of affection and compassion;
even that which is prohibited is permitted for a compassionate person who perceives the greater purpose. (17)
Thus it is said. Furthermore,
one who has accumulated merit, extensive learning, and so forth, possesses a very firm conviction that all phenomena are like illusions and dreams, having the single flavor of emptiness.
How could there even be a scent of contradiction between that [monastic discipline] and the *vajradhara* vow?
For this very reason, the Blessed One stated, "One should make a monk a *vajradhara*," and this must necessarily be accepted.

Otherwise, how would one reconcile the Vinaya teaching that a monk—who, due to the simultaneous awakening of the latencies (*vāsanā*) of both, sees a dream and experiences pleasure while experiencing everything up to the pleasure of the two external organs during a dream seen by his consort who likewise experiences pleasure—is nonetheless free from transgression? This must be established.

If, however, the location should be a domain of wicked people, then even for such a person the secret empowerment and the wisdom-knowledge empowerment (*prajñājñāna-abhiṣeka*) should be conferred by means of the knowledge-seal (*jñānamudrā*).
But in the absence of wicked people, [they should be conferred] by means of the action-seal (*karmamudrā*) alone.

However, for a monk who has not attained firmness regarding reality and liberation—even if he is faithful—the reception of empowerment by means of an external wisdom-woman (*bāhyaprajñā*) is forbidden.
Otherwise, there would be great misfortune due to the loss of one's previous vows.

However, if the Guru is a stable practitioner, then when the Wisdom-Seal (*jñānamudrā*) has been offered by him, the Wisdom-Consecration (*prajñābhiṣeka*) should also be given; and for the disciple who has taken [the vow], there is not even a suspicion of non-celibacy, because of the absence of physical action.

For that disciple, however, the distinctions such as "joy" (*ānanda*) and so forth must be demonstrated by means of recollecting the pleasure experienced previously during the state of being a householder.

Even if the guru is a monk, all that has been said regarding the bestowing of the secret initiation and so forth should be applied here; enough with this digression—let us speak of the subject at hand.

Thereafter, having instructed the disciples—who have replicated the maṇḍala, hold handfuls of flowers, placed their knees upon the ground, and are fit for the Mantra system—to enter the maṇḍala not merely for the sake of prosperity in this world nor for prosperity in the next, but for the attainment of the perfection of the three bodies (*kāyatraya*) of the Tathāgata, [the master] should announce: "If it is done thus, both types of prosperity will come to be. Then, having mentally caused those disciples to enter his own body through his mouth, they emerge from his own vajra as his own manifestations.

Having visualized [the disciples] being consecrated by the Tathāgatas together with their vidyās, who have been drawn in by rays from the seed-syllable at the heart and entered through the mouth, having melted, one should seat them at the eastern gate of the mandala and have them request entry:
"O Great Joy, you are my Teacher, the sole deliverer from the ocean of existence, which is terrifying with death, birth, old age, sickness, and other such [sufferings]. (18)
O Great Lord, I desire the firm path of great awakening;
grant me the reality of the samaya, and grant me the bodhicitta.
Grant me the three refuges: the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
O Lord, lead me into the supreme city of great liberation.
Teaching thus, he then made one disciple the principal and said:
"Come, child, [to this] method of the Mahāyāna, the way of mantra practice."
I shall teach you correctly, for you are a worthy vessel for the Great Vehicle.
The Buddhas, arisen throughout the three times, are devoid of body, speech, and mind;
they have attained incomparable gnosis through the cultivation of vajra mantras. (22)
By means of this incomparable application of mantra, the exceedingly terrible and mighty army of Māra was shattered by the forces of the Lion of the Śākyas and others. (23)
Having conformed to worldly convention and having set the wheel in motion, they have attained liberation;
therefore, my child, apply this mind toward the attainment of omniscience. (24)
Having thus recited it himself, he then says:
"The Three Jewels are my refuge; I confess all my misdeeds."
I rejoice in the merit of the world and fix my mind upon the enlightenment of a Buddha. // 25 //
Thus one should cause him to recite it three times.
Having thus caused the one who holds the general vows to receive the vows of an ācārya, and having bestowed the irreversible consecration of the [mandala] circle, one says: "O Lord, speak to me!"
The reality of the wheel and the deity, and the preparation of the preceptor. // 26 //
I shall always be the preceptor for the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings, [observing] the commitment of all Buddhas, the supreme secret vow. (27)
Having thus caused [the student] to perform the specific supplication, one should cause them to generate the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*):
"May all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas attend to me."

May the preceptor attend to me: I, [name], from this moment until sitting at the seat of enlightenment, generate the supreme, unsurpassed mind of awakening, just as the Protectors of the three times have made their resolve for perfect enlightenment. (28)
I firmly undertake the threefold training in ethical discipline, the gathering of virtuous qualities, and the ethical discipline of acting for the benefit of sentient beings. (29)
From this day forward, I shall undertake the vow born of the yoga of the Buddha with respect to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha—the supreme, unsurpassed Three Jewels. (30)
I accept the vajra, the bell, and the mudrā according to reality.
And I shall accept a master within the exalted Mahāvajra family. (31)
I shall bestow the fourfold gift six times every day,
within the worthy Great Jewel Family, at a delightful and auspicious time.
I receive the True Dharma—outer and secret, belonging to the three vehicles—within the pure Great Lotus family, which is a great ocean of awakening. (33)
I accept the vow associated with all [deities] from every source, performing acts of worship according to my ability within the great accumulation of the family of action. (34)
I generate the supreme, unsurpassed mind of awakening, having taken up the complete vow for the sake of the benefit of all sentient beings. (35)
I shall ferry across those who have not crossed; I shall liberate those who are not liberated;
I shall give rest to those who are weary, and I shall establish all beings in final nirvana.

Having had them recite this three times, one should then protect them with the Amṛtakuṇḍalī mantra. Then, having visualized the syllables *HŪṂ*, *ĀḤ*, and *OṂ*—black, red, and white respectively—situated upon the sun, sun, and moon disks atop a vajra, lotus, and wheel at their hearts, throats, and heads, and while uttering those syllables, one should touch the heart, throat, and head with the left fist holding a vajra moistened with scented water. One should then offer a flower on the head, incense and a lamp in front, and again scent at the heart.

Then, he should give to the disciples a tooth-stick (*dantakāṣṭha*) made of *aśvattha* wood or similar, twelve finger-breadths long, straight, unblemished, free from cuts, washed with fragrant water, and with a flower tied to its tip.
They, facing either east or north within a four-cubit square mandala smeared with cow dung and other substances, [should use] that tooth-stick while reciting:
*oṃ vajrahāsa hūṃ*.
Having recited thus, and having chewed [the tooth-stick] from the front, they tear it off and, looking upward, cast it away without regard, facing toward the [mandala].
According to where their tooth-stick falls, one should declare their future success:

by falling toward the east, north, west, south, upward, downward, or face-down, there are respectively the successes of pacification (śānti), enrichment (puṣṭi), subjugation (vaśya), malevolent rites (abhicāra), the state of a Vidyādhara, and the Pātāla; however, if it falls outside the mandala, there is no success.

Thereafter, having given water consecrated with the syllable *vaṃ* and recited over it for the purpose of sipping (*ācamana*), or else three handfuls of scented water consecrated seven times by means of the *kuṇḍalī*, one should make [the disciple] drink it while reciting:
"Oṃ hrīḥ! O Pure Dharma, purify all the sins of this person; remove all conceptual constructions, hūṃ!"

Then, having seated them outside, one should give many *kuśa* grasses with unbroken tips— either consecrated with the *hūṃ-jā* mantra or consecrated by the *Kuṇḍalinī*— for the purpose of spreading as a mat and a pillow,
with the mantra: *oṃ vajratīkṣṇa vaṃ*.

Thereafter, a thread spun by a maiden, equal in length to the body of the disciple and tripled, is tied with three knots using the Amṛtakuṇḍalin mantra; this should be placed on their left arm—for women, on both arms—with the mantra:
*Oṃ buddhamaitrī rakṣa rakṣa sarvān svāhā*.
Reciting thus, having bound it himself, he should properly protect and encourage [others].
Whatever evil was committed previously over many millions of eons, all that indeed goes to destruction upon seeing such a maṇḍala. (37)
The occurrence of all suffering and the miserable states of existence are destroyed for those whose minds are utterly pure regarding this supreme practice. (38)
Today, O great-souled ones, you have obtained incomparable gains, in that you have been admitted here into the teaching of all the Victors together with their sons. (39)
All those who are born having been taken up by great beings will indeed be well-born in the Mahāyāna because of that. 40.
This is the glorious, supreme path, the great success of the Mahāyāna, by which you, proceeding along it, shall become Tathāgatas. (41)
Having thus caused them to hear this, he should then protect the area with the Kuṇḍalī-mantra; having explained the Kuṇḍalī-mantra for the purpose of their recitation, he should say:
"Whatever dream you see, you shall tell me all of it in the morning.
Having spoken thus, he should have them sleep inside the mandala-hall, separated by a curtain or the like, or elsewhere on a lion-bed.
Having entered the maṇḍala house oneself, one should recite the Kuṇḍalī mantra for the sake of protection.
Here, that vow (*saṃvara*) which is granted even without making someone an *ācārya* is the common one, characterized merely by taking refuge and generating the bodhicitta.
However, that which is granted in order to make someone an *ācārya* is the *ācārya*-vow, which is comprised of the five families.
Therefore, this is the procedure for the preparation (*adhivāsana*) of the disciples, preceded by the bestowal of the two vows (*saṃvara*).

Thereafter, at dawn, the Guru, having offered the sacrificial oblation (*bali*) and emerged from the maṇḍala house, shall ask the disciples about their dreams. If an inauspicious dream is indicated by such things as falling from a mountain, he shall protect them with the Kuṇḍalī mantra. Then, at the time of re-entering the maṇḍala house, together with the disciples...

"Oṃ, enter, O Blessed One, the city of liberation of great bliss, which bestows the bliss of all accomplishments; O supreme, most excellent bliss, be accomplished! Jaḥ hūṃ vāṃ hoḥ, may you be fully perfected!
Having been thus encouraged, the Lord of Yogins then arises, his eyes wide open and radiant.
Having performed a circumambulation of the wheel, one should begin the opening of the door. // 42 //
Standing at the western gate, vibrating with the pratyālīḍha posture,
one should open the eastern door while reciting the mantra *vajrahūṃkāra* along with its mudrā.
Oṃ, open the vajra! Enter into the pledge! Hūṃ!
Reciting thus, while stationed in the northern direction and maintaining the wrathful gaze, one should open the southern door and release the wrathful mudrā. (44)
The yogin, stationed in the eastern direction and likewise facing westward,
having opened the western gate, should release the krodha-mudrā.
Likewise, staying in the southern direction, one should proceed clockwise as before;
having opened the door presided over by Dhanada, one should enter again in this manner. (46)
Oṃ, with these most graceful and playful gestures born of the intention for supreme bliss, I bow to the Blessed One:
Jaḥ Hūṃ Vaṃ Hoḥ Hi Hi Hi Hi Hīḥ! O Lord, accept this handful of flowers!
Having cast it into the maṇḍala with the mantra "Hoḥ," and having bound it again upon one's own head with the intention of a garland-consecration, one should visualize the Guru as the manifest wheel.

Having received from him the entire series of consecrations to be described hereafter, beginning with the garland and water consecrations, and having obtained authorization for all the duties of a preceptor according to the ritual rules, he should, for the sake of admitting the disciple, aspire toward the accomplishment of the mandala preceded by a praise of the reality consisting of wisdom and means whose nature is great bliss, and he should perform the empowerment of truth (*satyādhiṣṭhāna*):
"O Supreme Being, consisting of the Great Vajra, without beginning or end because your signs arise in space; O Akṣobhyavajra and others, grant me success! (47)
May the King who holds all vajras, the supreme among all great siddhis, the presiding deity of sovereignty, and the supreme syllable, grant me accomplishment. // 48 //
You are faultless and eternal, the one who inspires passion for all passions; O Blessed One, as such, grant me accomplishment through the reality of great passion and great delight. 49.
The Tathāgata, the supreme of utterly pure phenomena, liberated from the beginning, Samantabhadra, the self of all—may the Bodhisattva grant me success! 50.
Through the supreme mudrā of sovereignty, which is the greatest of all great accomplishments, my vajra-arrogance is manifested by the great excellence of the perfected vajra. (51)

Pervading the minds of all sentient beings, abiding in the hearts of all sentient beings, he is indeed the father of all sentient beings and the foremost among those who hold the supreme samaya of desire. // 52 //
By that truth through which my wisdom—the maṇḍala whose nature is both insight and skillful means—has arisen, by that truth, O Protector, may you fulfill my desires. (53)
They share the same nature as reflections; they are transparent, pure, and unclouded;
they are ungraspable and inexpressible, arising from causes and karma. // 54 //
By the truth that suchness is born from reality, may all disciples, free from stain, behold the mandala clearly as a reflection. (55)
Reciting thus, one should perform the *satyādhiṣṭhāna* (empowerment by truth); this is the entry of the master.

Then, having placed the initiated disciple—who observes the two vows—behind a curtain at the eastern door, and having purified him with fragrant substances and the like, he should be visualized in the form of Vairocana or in the form of the Lord of the Mandala (*cakrādhipa*).
With the mantra *oṃ sarvatathāgatānuttarabodhyalaṃkālavastrapūjāmeghasamudraspharaṇasamaye hūṃ*, [one offers] a red garment or another [garment] that has been prepared as a lower robe; then,
*oṃ vajrarakṣa haṃ*.
Having thus donned the upper garment,
he dons the uṣṇīṣa with the mantra: *oṃ vajroṣṇīṣa hūṃ phaṭ*.
With the mantra *oṃ cakṣurbandhavaram ānaya hūṃ*, the blindfold is bound;

with *āḥ khaṃ vīra hūṃ*, he is given a flower garland, has offered the ritual fee (*dakṣiṇā*), and is led forward by a Yoginī or by the Karmavajrī holding water from the all-purpose flask (*sārvakarmika-kalaśa*).
Then he should ask his own disciple: "Who are you, O lover of the rite?
Thereupon, the disciple should reply: "I am fortunate, possessed of great bliss."
Then,
having caused him to generate the thought of awakening by reciting "Oṃ, I generate the mind of all yoga," he places the vajra together with a flower at his heart.
Reciting "Oṃ surate samayas tvaṃ hoḥ sidhya vajra yathāsukham," and having held [it], [the master says]:
"Today you shall be empowered by all the Tathāgatas."
And you must not speak of this supreme secret of all the Tathāgatas to one who has not entered the mandala, nor to one who lacks faith; having said this,
recite "Oṃ Āḥ Yamāntakṛt Hūṃ" while drawing [the disciple] in.
Having caused [him] to enter within the curtain with "ĀḤ KHAṂ VĪRA HŪṂ," [one should proceed].

Circumambulating while reciting, "O Great Joy, O Very Firm One, O Well-pleased One, O Most Blissful One! O Vajrasattva, grant me accomplishment today! and with palms joined, he should prostrate toward the eastern gate of the maṇḍala with arms outstretched, uttering this mantra:
*oṃ sarvatathāgatapūjopasthānāyātmānaṃ niryātayāmi*.
Empowered by all the Tathāgatas and Vajrasattva, [I pray:
Oṃ, I offer myself for the service of worship to all the Tathāgatas.
Empower me, O Vajravairocana of all the Tathāgatas!
At the heart on the right, with palms joined:
*oṃ sarvatathāgatapūjābhiṣekāyātmānaṃ niryātayāmi*.
Consecrate me with the vajra-jewel empowerment of all the Tathāgatas.
In the west, with palms joined at the forehead:
Oṃ, I offer myself for the sake of setting in motion the worship of all Tathāgatas.
O Vajradharma of all Tathāgatas, set me in motion!
In the north, at the heart, with palms joined:
*Oṃ, for the sake of the ritual of worship of all Tathāgatas, I offer myself.
O Vajra-action of all Tathāgatas, act for me!*

Having thus paid homage to the Tathāgatas, Akṣobhya and the others, with these five mantras, one should again extend the arms toward the eastern door and say: "Oṃ, I offer myself for attendance at the feet of the Guru.
Oṃ, I offer myself for the sake of protecting all sentient beings."
Thus one should cause [the student] to recite, preceded by a comprehension of the meaning.
Then...

"Today you have entered the family of all the Tathāgatas; therefore, I shall generate in you the vajra-wisdom by which you will attain even the accomplishments of all the Tathāgatas, let alone other accomplishments. You must not speak of this before anyone who has not seen the maṇḍala, lest your samaya be violated.
Having said this, he places the vajra upon [the disciple's] head and rings the bell.
"This is your vow: the vajra shall split your head if you should speak of this to anyone.
Having said this, he again placed the vajra at his heart and said:
"Vajrasattva himself is now established within your heart."
If one should speak this method, one would depart at that very moment, having pierced through [the obstacles].

Having thus caused him to take an oath, one should give the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) contained in a lotus vessel, consecrated with the three-syllable mantra and placed atop the victory flask (*vijayakalaśa*),
by pouring it from the mouth of the vessel held between the ring finger and thumb into his own mouth, while reciting "Oṃ vajrāmṛtodaka ṭhaḥ" seven times.
This water of hell shall burn you for transgressing the pledge;
through the preservation of the pledge, there is accomplishment. Drink this vajra-amṛta water! (58)
Having recited this and caused [the disciple] to drink from the vessel, [the master says]:
"From this day forward, I am Vajrapāṇi to you; whatever I say, 'Do this,' must be performed by you.
You must not disregard me, lest through failing to avoid poison you meet your end and fall into hell."
Thus he should speak. This is the offering of the water of the pledge (samayodaka).
Then, with a concentrated mind, the disciple should repeat [the mantra] for the sake of his own immersion (svāveśa).
She spoke these words as instructed by the Teacher for the sake of accomplishing all siddhis. // 59 //
"May all the Tathāgatas empower [me], and may Vajrasattva enter into me.
Then:
Having meditated on the body as being hollow from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head, one should then visualize below it the circle of fire together with the wind.
Above that, one should visualize the syllable *jhraiḥ* of red color;
with the streams of light rays arising from it, the practitioner should purify his body. (61)
Having thus rendered [the disciple] radiant, the adept, for the sake of emergence, should repeatedly perform the placement of *hūṃ*, *haḥ*, and *āḥ* upon the disciple’s heart, throat, and head. (62)
Holding the bell that causes possession, the practitioner should ring it with grandeur;
for the purpose of invoking the Tathāgatas' descent, he should utter this mantra. (63)
"This is your vajra commitment, known as Vajrasattva;
today itself it shall cause the supreme vajra-wisdom to enter you. (64)
Oṃ vajrāveśa aḥ aḥ aḥ! If [the deity] does not enter even while reciting this mantra firmly, then one should impel the Jñānasattva with rays of light from the syllable ĀḤ. // 65 //
"Enter! Shake! Ra ra ra ra! Move! Move! Hūṃ haḥ āḥ jaiḥ!
One should recognize the signs of possession as being trembling, horripilation, fainting, dancing, or even falling backward. (66)
Having seen the disciple of Viṣṭaraśravas, one should place the syllable ĀḤ on the tongue;
having stabilized it with the hundred-syllable mantra, the adept should inquire about what is auspicious or inauspicious.
Having brought [the deity] by means of this sequence of entry, the knower of mantras,
having drawn in the descended deity with rays from his own heart and absorbed it into the seed-syllable in his own heart, should hold a vajra upon the head of the disciple and say:
"Oṃ, you have been made..."
Following these preliminary steps, one should dismiss [the deities] with the mantra: *hūṃ haḥ āḥ jhaiḥ muḥ*.
Thus ends the procedure for the descent of power (*āveśa*).
1. The Empowerment of Knowledge (*vidyābhiṣeka*).

[1. Mālābhiṣeka] Then, having asked the disciple facing the maṇḍala, "What kind of appearance do you perceive before your eyes? and having ascertained his suitability for the rites of pacification, enrichment, subjugation, or wrathful activity according to the sequence of the appearances he describes—whether white, yellow, red, dark green, or black—the master should take him by both thumbs with his right hand holding a vajra. While performing the dance of the vajra-steps and reciting the Kuṇḍalī mantra, he should cause him to circumambulate three times and then perform the empowerment through truth (*satyādhiṣṭhāna*).
Thus, this disciple has been correctly initiated by me into the maṇḍala;
may he possess the lineage of the deities and merit accordingly. // 1 //
Whatever kind of accomplishment may arise for him, in whatever lineage and in whatever vessel, and whatever the power of his merit may be—let that same [attainment] be his within this mandala. //2//
Having thus performed the empowerment through truth (*satyādhiṣṭhāna*),

one should then pluck a single fresh, small flower from the previously taken garland that has been consecrated with the syllable *trāṃ*, and place it in the hollowed palms of the disciple. At that time, he should resolve that his own self, radiant with the three syllables, is free from all defilement, and [resolve] that garland of flowers to be likewise.

Having been thus empowered by the Guru, [the disciple] should take hold of the Lord of the Mandala—who stands before him as if present, together with the members of the mandala (*maṇḍaleya*)—and, having mentally entered that mandala, he should cast a flower upon his head while reciting this mantra:

*Oṃ tiṣṭha vajra! Be firm for me; be eternal for me. Empower my heart; grant me all accomplishments! Hūṃ ha ha ha ha hoḥ āḥ kaṃ vīra hūṃ! O Lord, accept this handful of flowers! Hoḥ!* While reciting this mantra, the Guru should assign the disciple’s *kula* (family) according to the spot where the flower falls within the five lines of the mandala.
One should bestow that yoga and observe the attainment of success (*siddhi*).
If the flower falls upon the *uṣṇīṣa* or the *ūrṇā* on the heads of the Buddhas, then there is the attainment of the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā-siddhi*).
If it falls upon the eyes or the mouth, then there is the attainment of the Mantra (*mantra-siddhi*).

If it falls on the head, it is excellent; on the middle part of the body, middling; but on the lower part, it is inferior. If it falls at a great distance from the image, success will come after a long time; if near, success is swift. Regarding the deities, however, one's own station—such as the heart and so forth—should be understood by its location.
If the flower falls between two deities, then whichever deity is closer to the flower, that is the one's family (kula).

But when there is equality, the rule for both is established. Then, whichever [line] he prefers becomes his *kula*. If, however, the throw falls outside the five lines, one should cast again up to three times.
In that case, if one falls outside [the inner circle], there is a minor accomplishment (*kṣudrasiddhi*).
If one falls outside the outer vajra-garland among the outer circular lines, there is no accomplishment at all.
Furthermore, one must not show this mandala to such a person.
Having brought him to a state of fitness through mantra-recitation and other means, he should be introduced at another opportunity.
Then, taking that flower, one should say: "Oṃ, accept this being, O you of great power!"
Reciting thus, one should bind [the garland] upon the head of the disciple.
This is the procedure for the consecration with the garland (mālābhiṣeka-vidhi).
[The Procedure for the Entrance of the Disciple (śiṣyapraveśa-vidhi)]
When this possession has occurred, after explaining the auspicious signs and so forth,

one should stabilize the possession with the mantra "Oṃ tiṣṭha vajra," then perform the inquiry regarding the appearance of the eyes and so on, up until the binding of the head, and finally dismiss the descended deity.

They say that because of the lack of capacity [to perform the visualization], if the rite of possession (*āveśavidhi*) has not been performed, one should conduct the inquiry regarding the appearance of the eyes and so forth immediately after the offering of the water of commitment (*samayodaka*).
Following that, [one should place] something flaming upon the two eyes of the disciple.
Oṃ! Having meditated upon the duality, Vajrasattva himself is now intent on opening your eyes;
he, whose eyes are all-seeing, opens the unsurpassed Vajra-eye. (3)
Reciting "Oṃ jñānacakṣuḥ hūṃ aḥ svāhā," he should remove the blindfold.
Then...
Having said, "O Vajra, look! and "Look at this mandala and now generate faith," [he speaks].
You are born into the family of the Buddhas and are empowered by the mudrās and mantras. // 4 //
Through the perfection of all accomplishments, you shall become a supreme holder of the samaya;
perform the worship of mantras with the graceful play of the supreme Vajra and Lotus. (5)
Having recited thus, one should then reveal the reality of the mandala in its proper sequence,
and one should also instruct upon the essential nature of all the deities. (6)
It should have the four noble truths as its corners and the divine abodes as its vertices;
the means of attraction are called its gates, each being designated as "fourfold. (7)
The mind consisting of the faculty of faith and so forth arises from five ramparts;
the four bases of psychic power are the fourfold gateways. (8)
In its center, however, is the wheel which resembles eight mandalas;
this indeed is the eightfold liberation that accomplishes all siddhis. (9)
In this great mass of all accomplishments, they are always the pillars;
the Noble Eightfold Path is known as the eight pillars. (10)
The symbolic representation of the meaning of the *dharmadhātu* is the mandala within the wheel;
for this is the mind-mandala, the supreme city of great liberation. (11)
The meditative concentrations are the archways here, and likewise the primordial nature is the banners;
the trees of paradise at the gates are the fruits of perfect enlightenment.
One should manifest the five Buddhas by way of the nature of the five aggregates;
the four goddesses beginning with Locanā as having the nature of earth and the other elements;
and likewise Rūpavajrā and the others as having the nature of the five objects of desire. (13)
Furthermore, one should manifest Kṣitigarbha and the others with the nature of the eye and so forth, and the lords of wrath such as Yamāntaka and others in the form of the arms and so forth. // 14 //
One should compassionately reveal to the disciple the Buddhas, such as Akṣobhya and the others, who reside in the body-mandala in their proper order, within the external mandala. (15)
Thus:
"I have entered the great mandala of the Vajra-maṇḍala;
I have been shown the great mandala of the Yoga-maṇḍala."
"I have been initiated into the secret mandala and the great mandala. Having made him recite this, he should cause him to hear the pledge:
"Hoḥ! Hoḥ! Hoḥ!"

Thus concludes the procedure for the entrance of the disciple. [2. The Procedure for the Water Consecration] Then, for the sake of the water consecration, having given a fee to the guru according to one's means, with knees placed upon the ground and palms joined in reverence:
Just as the Great Festival was bestowed upon the Buddhas by Bodhivajra, for the sake of my protection as well, O Khavajra, grant it to me today! (16)
Reciting thus, one should make the request.
Then, outside the mandala, in the eastern direction, there is a mandala.
Or, in the northeast, the mantra-practitioner should draw a four-cornered square with four openings.
It should be two cubits in size and consist of two layers; in its center is a universal lotus, and one should draw three enclosures in white, red, and black.

Having established the wheel in the eastern quarter, the jewel in the southern, the lotus with its filaments in the western, and the universal vajra of the Giver of Wealth (Kubera) in the northern, one should place the ritual vases.
Thus ends the procedure for the bathing mandala.
Having brought that disciple who has performed the Kṛtamālā consecration, one should establish him in the center of the lotus within the mandala, as the one who bears the deity within his womb. (20)
The preceptor, together with his retinue, should perform the consecration for the vajra-disciple using the jars drawn forth, reciting verses preceded by auspicious benedictions. (21)
Like white pods full [of seeds], the Jinas, bearing water-pots, shall today consecrate you, knowing thus your state of benevolence. (22)
Having spoken thus, one should perform the *nīrājana* rite for the disciple—who has been visualized in the form of Vajradhara—according to the previously mentioned procedure.

Thereafter, having summoned the Tathāgatas and the Knowledge Goddesses residing in the infinite directions by means of rays from the seed-syllable in the heart, and having worshipped them, [one should recite]:
"The consecration of the Buddhas by the Vajrin is indeed for the protection of the world."
Give to him exactly as you have been given. For this is so. // 23 //

Having thus supplicated with this verse, those Tathāgatas, having entered into meditative absorption on wisdom and melted by great passion, enter within through the door of Vairocana and proceed by way of the vajra-path.
